questions.knowledge_point: The Parametric Equations of an Ellipse Centered at a General Point
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14032117/assets/14d1fc5a92c28cc7f84c1ec23929701f1aca67b1a15d6113fa83f1428354fc11.png)

Consider the ellipse centered at $(3,-1)$ with horizontal radius $2$ and vertical radius $3,$ as shown above. Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $\theta \in [0,2\pi ),$  traverse the ellipse once in the counterclockwise direction starting at the point $A(5,-1)?$
questions.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of an ellipse centered at the point $(h,k)$ with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ are

$$
x=a\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +h,\,y=b\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +k,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

Under this parametrization, the ellipse is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction, starting from $(h+a,k).$

In our case, the ellipse is centered at the point $(3,-1),$ $a=2$ and $b=3.$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the ellipse are 

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +3,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -1,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14032117/assets/4e9218dcfc77ec080139f2650ea19f78199557e0ce2d8d53c1996ec0ea6145a6.png)

The half-ellipse above is defined by the parametric equations 

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

What is the domain of the parameter $\theta ?$
questions.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ are

$$
x=a\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=b\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

In our case, $a=3$ and $b=2.$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the *full* ellipse are

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

To restrict the parameterization to a half-ellipse, we associate the parameter $\theta $ with the central angle formed by a point $(x,y)$ on the elipse and the $x$-axis. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14032117/assets/dfbe843a9ad0847d7174984fa7c7c48834af48b3ee2335b5383b15f7fb826763.png)

We can see that if we restrict $\theta $ to $[\pi ,2\pi ]$, we get the half-ellipse.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the half-ellipse are 

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [\pi ,2\pi ].
$$

questions.knowledge_point: The Cartesian Equation of an Ellipse
questions.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the ellipse

$$
x=5\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0\le \theta <2\pi .
$$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the ellipse, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By isolating the $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =5\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{x}{5} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{5}^{2}} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{25} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By isolating the $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{y}{4} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{4}^{2}} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{16} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

 
Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{25}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the ellipse is

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{25}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}=1.
$$

$$

In our case, $a=4$ and $b=2.$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the *full* ellipse are

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

To restrict the parameterization to a quarter-ellipse, we associate the parameter $\theta $ with the central angle formed by a point $(x,y)$ on the ellipse and the $x$-axis. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14032117/assets/fb686f7295c2c6ac3058361ecc0438ae56d650950833185b17ec959d654cc511.png)

$$

questions.knowledge_point: The Cartesian Equation of an Ellipse
questions.problem:
The Cartesian equation of the ellipse defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=6\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=11\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,0\le \theta <2\pi .
$$

is given by

{{field-1}}
$=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the ellipse, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$  We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By isolating the $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =6\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{x}{6\sqrt{2}} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{(6\sqrt{2})^{2}} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{72} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By isolating the $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =11\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{y}{11} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{11}^{2}} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{121} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{72}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{121}={cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1.
$$

So, the Cartesian equation of the ellipse is

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{72}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{121}=1.
$$
